questions.question: A chocolate bar is one whole. It is broken into 3 equal parts and 1 part is eaten. That is the fraction 1/3. Which decimal is EXACTLY equal to 1/3?
options: 0.3 with a bar over the 3
questions.explain: 1 ÷ 3 = 0.3333... and the 3s never stop, so it is a repeating decimal written as 0.3 with a bar over the 3. Stopping at 0.33 or 0.333 is only a rounded value, not the exact amount.

questions.question: Each of these describes one whole cut into equal parts with some parts shaded. Which one gives a TERMINATING decimal?
options: 1 shaded out of 6 equal parts
5 shaded out of 8 equal parts
2 shaded out of 3 equal parts
5 shaded out of 9 equal parts
questions.explain: A decimal terminates when the division ends: 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625 and stops. The trap is thinking 1/6, 2/3 and 5/9 stop too — they give 0.1666..., 0.6666... and 0.5555..., which repeat forever.

questions.question: One whole is divided into 9 equal parts and 4 parts are shaded, so the fraction is 4/9. Dividing gives 4 ÷ 9 = 0.4444... Which is the correct bar notation for this decimal?
options: 0.4 with a bar over the 4
questions.explain: The bar goes over the digit that keeps repeating, so 0.4444... is written 0.4 with a bar over the 4. Writing 0.44 or 0.444 chops the decimal off and turns a repeating decimal into a terminating one, which changes its value.

questions.question: One whole is divided into 11 equal parts and 3 parts are shaded, so the fraction is 3/11. Dividing gives 3 ÷ 11 = 0.272727... Which statement is true?
options: It is terminating and equals 0.27 exactly.
It is terminating and equals 0.2727 exactly.
It is repeating, written as 0.272727 with a bar over the 2 only.
It is repeating, written as 0.27 with a bar over both digits, 27.
questions.explain: The block 27 repeats forever, so the bar must cover the whole repeating block: 0.27 with a bar over 27. A bar over the 2 alone would mean 0.2722222..., and cutting it off at 0.27 or 0.2727 pretends a repeating decimal terminates.

questions.question: Without doing the long division, which fraction is a terminating decimal?
questions.explain: Break the denominator into prime factors: 40 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 5, only 2s and 5s, so 7/40 terminates (0.175). The trap is 30, 15 and 60 — each still has a factor of 3, so those decimals repeat (0.2333..., 0.4666..., 0.11666...) instead of stopping.

questions.question: At hockey practice Owen scored on 5 of his 12 shots. Written as an exact decimal, what is 5/12?
options: 0.41 with a bar over the 6
0.416 with a bar over the digits 416
questions.explain: 5 ÷ 12 = 0.41666..., where only the 6 repeats, so the bar goes over the 6 alone: 0.41 with a bar over the 6. Rounding to 0.42 or stopping at 0.416 treats a repeating decimal as if it terminates.

questions.question: Liam ate 3 of the 8 granola bars in his box. Ava ate 3 of the 9 granola bars in her box. Whose fraction is a repeating decimal?
options: Both of them, because both fractions have a 3 in them
Only Liam's, because 3/8 = 0.375
Only Ava's, because 3/9 = 0.3 with a bar over the 3
Neither one, because both decimals stop after a few digits
questions.explain: Check each division: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 and stops, while 3 ÷ 9 = 0.3333... and never stops, so only Ava's repeats. Having a 3 in the numerator does not matter — what matters is whether the division ends.

questions.question: Three friends share a $10 pizza equally, so each share is 10 ÷ 3 dollars. Which statement is true?
options: Each share is exactly $3.33.
The answer terminates, because money can only have two decimal places.
Each share is exactly $3.3.
10 ÷ 3 = 3.3 with a bar over the 3, a repeating decimal, so $3.33 is only a rounded amount.
questions.explain: 10 ÷ 3 = 3.3333..., a repeating decimal written as 3.3 with a bar over the 3, so $3.33 is a rounded price, not the exact share. Money is rounded to cents for convenience — that rounding does not make the decimal terminate.

questions.question: Priya divides 2 ÷ 11 on her calculator and the screen shows 0.1818181818. She says the decimal terminates because the screen stops. Which statement is correct?
options: She is wrong; the screen only fits so many digits. 2/11 = 0.18 with a bar over the 18, and it never ends.
She is right; the decimal terminates once you reach 0.18.
She is right; 2/11 equals 0.1818181818 exactly.
She is wrong; 2/11 = 0.18 with a bar over the 8, which never ends.
questions.explain: A calculator screen has limited space, so a cut-off display is not proof that a decimal ends; 2 ÷ 11 repeats the block 18 forever, written 0.18 with a bar over 18. Putting the bar over the 8 alone would mean 0.188888..., a different number.

questions.question: In Jayden's class, 15 of the 24 students walk to school. Jayden says 15/24 must be a repeating decimal, because 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 3 is not a 2 or a 5. Who is right?
options: Jayden is right: any denominator with a factor of 3 gives a repeating decimal.
Jayden is wrong: 15/24 simplifies to 5/8, and 8 = 2 × 2 × 2, so it terminates at 0.625.
Jayden is wrong: the 2s-and-5s test only works when the numerator is 1.
Jayden is right, and the decimal is 0.625 with a bar over the 5.
questions.explain: Always simplify the fraction first, then look at the prime factors of the denominator: 15/24 = 5/8, and 8 has only 2s, so the decimal terminates at 0.625. The common trap is testing the unsimplified denominator 24 and seeing a factor of 3 that actually cancels out.

questions.question: Marcus made 2 of his 3 free throws at the community centre. The score sheet lists his rate as 67%. Which statement about 2/3 is true?
options: 2/3 = 0.66 exactly, so his rate is exactly 66%.
2/3 = 0.67 exactly, so his rate is exactly 67%.
2/3 = 0.6 with a bar over the 6, so the exact percent is 66.6 with a bar over the 6 percent, and 67% is a rounded value.
2/3 = 0.666, so his rate is exactly 66.6%.
questions.explain: 2 ÷ 3 = 0.6666... forever, so the exact percent also repeats: 66.6 with a bar over the 6 percent, and 67% on the sheet is just rounded. The trap is believing the rounded number printed on a score sheet is the true, terminating value.

questions.question: Noah claims: ‘If the denominator ends in 5 or 0, the decimal always terminates.’ Which example proves his claim is wrong?
options: 7/15 = 0.46 with a bar over the 6
questions.explain: A counterexample must repeat, and 7 ÷ 15 = 0.4666..., which is written 0.46 with a bar over the 6 — so ending in 5 is not enough. What really matters is that the simplified denominator has only 2s and 5s as prime factors, and 15 = 3 × 5 still has a 3.
